meta.title: Who really said "Things turn out best for the people who make the best of the way things turn out"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not John Wooden's line. Quote Investigator traces it to an anonymous 1961 Illinois newspaper filler; Wooden printed it unattributed in 1973 and got the credit.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Things turn out best for the people who make the best of the way things turn out'?
meta.ogDescription: Anonymous newspaper filler from March 1961. John Wooden used a variant as an unattributed chapter epigraph in They Call Me Coach (1973) and has been credited ever since.

answer.label: Not John Wooden’s line — an anonymous saying he made famous
answer.authorDates: In print by 26 March 1961 · newspaper humor-column filler, Illinois
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ traced the adage to a one-line filler credited only to an unnamed “Ad Boy,” as collected by the column’s signature “PF Pete,” run in the humor column of two Illinois community newspapers on 26 March 1961. John Wooden did print the saying — as the epigraph to chapter 10 of They Call Me Coach (Bantam, 1973) — but he gave it no ascription and never claimed to have coined it. QI’s conclusion: the aphorism “has an anonymous origin,” and Wooden (like Art Linkletter after him) only popularized it.

source.excerpt: Ad Boy: Things turn out for the best for those who make the best out of the way things turn out. PF Pete
trail: 26 March 1961 — the earliest instance anyone has located: an unascribed one-liner in the humor columns of two Illinois community newspapers, credited only to an unnamed “Ad Boy,” per Quote Investigator ↗. Over the next decade it recurs in a Texas bank advertisement, a Boys’ Life reader submission and a West Virginia supermarket ad — never with a real, named author, only “Uncle Joe,” a Scoutmaster, or nobody at all.

1973 — John Wooden opens chapter 10 of They Call Me Coach ↗ with the saying, in the “those” form and with no ascription. QI cites the Bantam edition, p. 71, and notes the front matter records a Word Books edition published December 1972.

1977–1979 — newspapers begin printing it flatly as “John Wooden,” and Art Linkletter’s Yes, You Can quotes the “the people” wording while crediting Wooden — the step that fixed the modern form and the modern byline together, per QI ↗.
2010 — a Goodreads page ↗ reassigns the line to Titus Livius; Wikiquote’s sourced Wooden page ↗, meanwhile, does not carry the saying at all.
source.excerptNote: The 1961 filler as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗, run the same day in two Illinois community papers. Note that this earliest form reads “turn out for the best for those” — the polished “the people” version came later.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can be asserted for the aphorism itself: its author is unknown and its earliest documented appearance is an unascribed 1961 newspaper filler, so there is no identifiable creator or estate to hold a claim — and nothing here supports treating it as public domain. The books that carry it remain in copyright as whole works: John Wooden and Jack Tobin’s They Call Me Coach (1972–73) and Art Linkletter’s Yes, You Can (1979). Separately, the name “John R. Wooden” is handled as licensed property by John Wooden Legacy LLC ↗.

author.name: John Wooden
author.heading: About John Wooden
author.metaLine: 1910–2010 · UCLA basketball coach & former English teacher
author.bio: John Robert Wooden (14 October 1910 – 4 June 2010) coached UCLA men’s basketball from 1948 to 1975, winning ten NCAA championships including seven in a row from 1967 to 1973, and was the first person enshrined in the Basketball Hall of Fame as both a player and a coach. Before Westwood he taught English at South Bend Central High School, and he built his coaching around aphorisms — his Pyramid of Success, his father’s maxims, and a working stock of borrowed proverbs he quoted freely without ever claiming to have written them. That habit is exactly why so many sayings he merely repeated now travel the internet under his name.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why it’s wrong
misattribution.intro: Three names ride this one sentence, and none of them can be shown to have written it. The saying was public property in American newspapers for years before any of them touched it.

items.why: Wooden did print it — as the unattributed epigraph to chapter 10 of They Call Me Coach (Bantam, 1973), a citation Quote Investigator says it verified with scans ↗. But QI records that “Wooden did not claim coinage, nor did he provide an ascription,” and documents the saying in print from March 1961 onward. Even the licensed John Wooden legacy site ↗ prints it under his name with no source.

A 2010 Goodreads page ↗ assigned the line to the Roman historian, still with no book or passage cited. Quote Investigator ↗: “QI has found no substantive support for crediting the dictum to Titus Livius; that linkage appeared relatively recently.” A modern English antimetabole is not a translation of anything.

items.tag: a repeater who cited his source
items.why: Linkletter used the adage in his 1979 book Yes, You Can: How to Succeed in Business and Life — and did the honest thing, explicitly attributing it to Wooden, per Quote Investigator ↗. He repeated it often enough afterward that some collections now credit him instead.

The form that circulates today — “…for the people who…” — is not the wording in Wooden’s book, which reads “Things turn out best for those who make the best of the way things turn out.” QI ↗ records the “the people” form in Linkletter’s 1979 quotation of Wooden, and by 2006 a further drift (“Things work out best for those who make the best of how things work out”) was also circulating under Wooden’s name.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: nobody knows who wrote it. The earliest instance anyone has found is an unascribed 1961 newspaper filler credited only to an unnamed “Ad Boy,” as collected by the column’s signature “PF Pete” — and Quote Investigator’s verdict ↗ is that “this aphorism has an anonymous origin. Both John Wooden and Art Linkletter helped to popularize the saying, but neither created it.”

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Wooden
lead: The line is built on antimetabole — the same handful of words (things, turn, out, best) reshuffled across the two halves of the sentence. That structure makes it feel engineered rather than stumbled upon, which is precisely why readers assume a named author must be behind it. In fact it behaved for years like what it was: unascribed newspaper filler, dropped into humor columns, a Texas bank advertisement, a Boys’ Life reader submission and a West Virginia supermarket ad, always without a real, named author — variously “Uncle Joe,” a Scoutmaster, or nobody at all.

What changed was a famous mouth. When Wooden used it as a chapter epigraph in his 1973 memoir, a sports editor reprinting quotations from that book presented the saying as Wooden’s within months, and by 1977 a Florida newspaper was printing it under his name outright. Art Linkletter then repeated it in his 1979 book Yes, You Can while carefully crediting Wooden — carrying the credit further, and picking up a share of it himself along the way.
context.detailsSummary: How the credit migrated, step by step
detailsBody: 1961–1970: the saying appears repeatedly in American newspapers with no author — ascribed variously to “Ad Boy,” “Uncle Joe,” a Scoutmaster, or nobody at all, per Quote Investigator’s citation list ↗.
1973: Wooden runs it as the chapter 10 epigraph of They Call Me Coach, unattributed. QI notes it verified this citation with scans.
1973–1977: a Georgia sports editor reprints it among quotations from the book; a Florida paper prints it flatly as “John Wooden.”
1979 onward: Linkletter quotes it while crediting Wooden; a 2010 Goodreads page hands it to the Roman historian Titus Livius instead, an attribution QI found no substantive support for.
context.pull: It was anonymous filler for twelve years. Then a famous coach printed it without a byline, and the byline filled itself in.
